questions.problem: Let $f(x,y,z)={e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(z).$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,1,\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,1,\pi )$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(0,1,\pi )+∇f(0,1,\pi )\cdot ⟨x,y-1,z-\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(0,1,\pi )=-1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =y{e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(0,1,\pi )=-1, \\ {f}_{y} & =x{e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(0,1,\pi )=0, \\ {f}_{z} & =-{e}^{xy}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(0,1,\pi )=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(0,1,\pi )$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(0,1,\pi ) & =⟨{f}_{x}(0,1,\pi ),{f}_{y}(0,1,\pi ),{f}_{z}(0,1,\pi )⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(0,1,\pi )+∇f(0,1,\pi )\cdot ⟨x,y-1,z-\pi ⟩ \\  & ≈-1+⟨-1,0,0⟩\cdot ⟨x,y-1,z-\pi ⟩ \\  & ≈-1-x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that $f(x,y,z)$ is a differentiable function such that

$$
f(2,-2,-1)=4,\,{f}_{x}(2,-2,-1)=2,\,{f}_{y}(2,-2,-1)=-2,\,{f}_{z}(2,-2,-1)=-4.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,-2,-1)$ estimate the value of $f(2.02,-1.98,-1.05)$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,-2,-1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,-2,-1)+∇f(2,-2,-1)\cdot ⟨x-2,y+2,z+1⟩ \\  & =f(2,-2,-1)+⟨{f}_{x}(2,-2,-1),{f}_{y}(2,-2,-1),{f}_{z}(2,-2,-1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y+2,z+1⟩ \\  & =4+⟨2,-2,-4⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y+2,z+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(2.02,-1.98,-1.05)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=2.02,$ $y=-1.98,$ and $z=-1.05$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2.02,-1.98,-1.05) & ≈4+⟨2,-2,-4⟩\cdot ⟨2.02-2,-1.98+2,-1.05+1⟩ \\  & =4+⟨2,-2,-4⟩\cdot ⟨0.02,0.02,-0.05⟩ \\  & =4+(0.04-0.04+0.2) \\  & =4.2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that $f(x,y,z)$ is a differentiable function such that

$$
\begin{aligned} & f(-3,-1,-2)=1, &  & {f}_{x}(-3,-1,-2)=4, \\  & {f}_{y}(-3,-1,-2)=-3, &  & {f}_{z}(-3,-1,-2)=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-3,-1,-2)$ estimate the value of $f(-3.04,-1.02,-2.03).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-3,-1,-2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(-3,-1,-2)+∇f(-3,-1,-2)\cdot ⟨x+3,y+1,z+2⟩ \\  & =f(-3,-1,-2) \\  & \,+⟨{f}_{x}(-3,-1,-2),{f}_{y}(-3,-1,-2),{f}_{z}(-3,-1,-2)⟩\cdot ⟨x+3,y+1,z+2⟩ \\  & =1+⟨4,-3,-2⟩\cdot ⟨x+3,y+1,z+2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(-3.04,-1.02,-2.03)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=-3.04,$ $y=-1.02,$ and $z=-2.03$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-3.04,-1.02,-2.03) & ≈1+⟨4,-3,-2⟩\cdot ⟨-3.04+3,-1.02+1,-2.03+2⟩ \\  & =1+⟨4,-3,-2⟩\cdot ⟨-0.04,-0.02,-0.03⟩ \\  & =1-0.16+0.06+0.06 \\  & =0.96\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that $f(x,y,z)$ is a differentiable function such that

$$
f(1,2,3)=6,\,{f}_{x}(1,2,3)=6,\,{f}_{y}(1,2,3)=3,\,{f}_{z}(1,2,3)=2.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,2,3)$ estimate the value of $f(1.08,1.93,3.05)$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,2,3)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,2,3)+∇f(1,2,3)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-2,z-3⟩ \\  & =6+⟨{f}_{x}(1,2,3),{f}_{y}(1,2,3),{f}_{z}(1,2,3)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-2,z-3⟩ \\  & =6+⟨6,3,2⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-2,z-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(1.08,1.93,3.05)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=1.08,$ $y=1.93,$ and $z=3.05$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.08,1.93,3.05) & ≈6+⟨6,3,2⟩\cdot ⟨1.08-1,1.93-2,3.05-3⟩ \\  & =6+⟨6,3,2⟩\cdot ⟨0.08,-0.07,0.05⟩ \\  & =6+6(0.08)+3(-0.07)+2(0.05) \\  & =6+0.48-0.21+0.1 \\  & =6.37\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f(x,y)={x}^{2}{e}^{y}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,0)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,0)+∇f(-1,0)\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-1,0)=1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =2x{e}^{y}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(-1,0)=-2, \\ {f}_{y} & ={x}^{2}{e}^{y} &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(-1,0)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-1,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,0) & =⟨-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,0)+∇f(-1,0)\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩ \\  & ≈1+⟨-2,1⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩ \\  & ≈1-2(x+1)+y \\  & ≈-1-2x+y.\end{aligned}
$$
